section.title: Cast Your Bread on the Waters
section.sectionRationale: As the book turns toward its close, the Teacher moves from diagnosis to counsel. Having shown that no one can master the future or read the hand of God, he does not collapse into paralysis. He commands bold, generous, diversified action precisely because the future is unknown. This is faith working in the dark, sowing seed while it is still morning.
section.thesis: Because you cannot know the future or trace the work of God, do not freeze; invest widely, give generously, and work diligently, trusting the God who alone knows what will prosper.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the call to cast your bread and divide your portion in the face of an unknown future, and the reminder that you cannot know the work of God, so sow your seed morning and evening and leave the outcome to Him.

units.label: Cast your bread, divide your portion

verses.text: Cast your {{lechem|bread}} upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again.
Divide your {{chelek|portion}} among seven, or even eight, for you do not know what disaster may befall the land.

units.label: You do not know the work of God

verses.text: If the clouds are full, they will pour out rain upon the earth; whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where it falls, there it will lie.
He who watches the wind will fail to sow, and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap.
As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the bones are formed in a mother’s womb, so you cannot understand the {{maaseh|work}} of God, the Maker of all things.
Sow your seed in the morning, and do not rest your hands in the evening, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper.

lechem.gloss: Bread, food, grain. To cast your bread upon the waters pictures a venture sent out where it seems lost, whether seaborne trade or grain scattered to sprout, that returns after many days. It commends risk and generosity rather than clutching what you have.

chelek.gloss: Portion, share, lot. The same word the Teacher uses through the book for the portion God gives a person to enjoy. Here he says to divide it among seven or eight, to spread it out, because no one can foresee which venture will survive the coming disaster.

maaseh.gloss: Work, deed, activity. A key word in Ecclesiastes for the work of God that a person cannot fully trace out. As you cannot map the wind or the forming of a child, so you cannot understand the work of God; that ignorance is meant to free you for faithful action, not freeze you.

basic.context: The Teacher has spent the whole book showing that we cannot control or predict what happens under the sun. Now he draws out what to do about it. Instead of telling us to give up, he tells us to act boldly and generously. Cast your bread on the waters. Spread your investments around, because you never know what disaster is coming. Do not stand around reading the weather forever, or you will never plant or harvest anything. Since you cannot understand the work of God any more than you can trace the wind or the making of a baby, get to work, sow in the morning and the evening, and leave the results to God.
basic.hermeneutics: These verses read like a short cluster of proverbs, and people have long debated whether the picture is mainly about generous charity or about bold, diversified enterprise. Either way the logic is the same: because the future is hidden and the work of God is beyond us, the wise response is not caution that never acts, but faith that acts and trusts. The refrain you do not know is meant to loosen our grip and free our hands, not tie them.
basic.originalLanguages: Cast your bread, lechem, upon the waters is a picture of sending something out that looks lost but comes back. Divide your portion, your cheleq, the very word the book uses for the share God gives you to enjoy. And the reason for all of it is that you cannot understand the work of God, His maaseh, the deeds only the Maker of all things fully knows.
basic.typology: The seed sown in hope of an unseen harvest runs through Scripture and points to Christ, who spoke of the sower and the seed and Himself became the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died to bear much fruit. The bread cast out and found again after many days hints at a generosity that God repays in His own time, fulfilled in the One who gave Himself away and was raised.
basic.christ: Jesus is the sower and the seed. He scattered the word of the kingdom knowing not all soil would receive it, and He Himself fell into the ground and died so that His life would multiply. He taught that giving, lending, and casting our bread out for others is stored up with God, who repays. The unknown future that unnerves us is the very hand of the Father who numbers our days.
basic.god: God is the Maker of all things, whose work is too deep to trace. He hides the future from us not to torment us but so that we will trust Him and act in faith. He is the one who gives the increase, who alone knows whether this venture or that will prosper, and He can be trusted with what we cannot see.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 11 says one who scatters yet increases. Second Corinthians 9 says the cheerful giver is supplied by God. Jesus tells of the sower in Mark 4 and the grain of wheat in John 12. James 4 warns against boasting about tomorrow, which we do not know.
basic.oneStory: The whole book has pressed the limits of human wisdom under the sun. Here that honesty turns into a summons: since we cannot master the future, we live by faith, sowing generously and leaving the harvest to God. It is the same faith that finds its ground in Christ, the seed that died and rose, in whom no labor is wasted.

context.literary:
The six verses are held together by a frame and a refrain. The frame is two imperatives about giving out: 'Cast your bread' in verse 1 and 'Sow your seed' in verse 6. In between, the refrain 'you do not know' falls three times, in verses 2, 5 and 6, each time as the reason for the command that precedes or follows it. The passage is built so that ignorance is never a reason to stop. It is always the reason to begin.

Inside the frame the verses pair off. Verses 1 and 2 are two commands of generous scattering, each with its reason: 'you will find it again' and 'you do not know what disaster may befall.' Verses 3 and 4 are two sayings about nature. The first says what can be known, that full clouds pour out rain and a fallen tree stays where it falls. The second draws the lesson that someone who waits on the wind and the clouds will never sow or reap. Verse 5 is the hinge, an analogy between the wind and the womb that says the work of God cannot be traced. Verse 6 closes with a command that recalls verse 1 in the language of the field.

The passage turns a corner in the book. Up to now the refrain of unknowing has been a complaint: no one can find out what is coming, 7:14, 8:7, 8:17, 9:12, 10:14. Here it becomes a ground for action. The same verb 'find' that was denied in 8:17, where no one can find out the work done under the sun, is granted in verse 1, where the one who casts his bread 'will find it again.' The mind cannot find God's work, but the hands will find their bread. The next verse, 11:7, opens the great closing movement on joy, remembering the Creator and the days of darkness, so these six verses form the doorway to the book's last chapters.
context.historical:
The images come from the two main economies of the world of the Teacher's hearers: trade and farming. Israel was not a great sea power, but its kings had a share in sea trade, such as Solomon's ships of Tarshish sailing with Hiram's fleet, 1 Kings 10:22, and the psalmist can speak of those who 'went out to sea in ships, conducting trade on the mighty waters,' Psalm 107:23. Sending goods across water meant long delays and real loss, so merchants had every reason to avoid putting all they had on one vessel. Some readers also note the practice in the Nile valley of scattering seed on flooded ground as the waters fell, and Isaiah 32:20 blesses 'those who sow beside abundant waters.' On this reading the image is of seed that seems lost on the surface of the flood and returns as a crop.

Farming made the same demand. Weather in Palestine could not be forced. Jesus notes that people read a cloud rising in the west and say a shower is coming, Luke 12:54, and a farmer who waited for perfect conditions could lose the whole season. The phrase 'seven, or even eight' belongs to a Hebrew way of speaking in which a number is followed by the next number to mean a full and generous list, as in Proverbs 6:16, Micah 5:5 and Job 5:19. It need not be taken as a rule of investment so much as an idiom for 'more than you think you need.'

The ignorance of the womb in verse 5 is a plain fact of the ancient world, where no one could see inside a woman's body. Job and the psalmist speak of the same mystery with awe, Job 10:8-11 and Psalm 139:13-16. And the risk of 'disaster upon the land,' drought, locusts, war or famine, was real and recurring, which gave the advice its force.
context.canonical:
The passage belongs with Israel's wisdom on giving. Proverbs says 'One gives freely, yet gains even more,' and 'A generous soul will prosper,' Proverbs 11:24-25, and that kindness to the poor 'is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender,' Proverbs 19:17. Isaiah says that if you give yourself to the hungry, 'your light will go forth in the darkness,' Isaiah 58:10, and the psalmist praises the righteous man who 'has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor,' Psalm 112:9.

The picture of sowing in hope is wider. 'Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy,' Psalm 126:5. The book's own emphasis on unknowing meets the wider Torah's: 'The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us,' Deuteronomy 29:29. We act on what is revealed and leave the rest.

The New Testament takes up both strands. Paul promises that whoever sows generously will reap generously and that God 'supplies seed to the sower and bread for food,' 2 Corinthians 9:6-10, and tells us not to grow weary in doing good because 'in due time we will reap a harvest,' Galatians 6:9. Jesus teaches the sower and the seed, Mark 4, and the grain that dies, John 12:24. He also takes the Teacher's point about not knowing: 'do not worry about tomorrow,' Matthew 6:34, and James warns that we do not know what will happen tomorrow, James 4:13-15. Both agree with the Teacher that planning is not wrong, but presumption about the future is.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher aimed at a particular kind of paralysis. A thoughtful person, having read the first ten chapters of his book, could easily conclude that since nothing can be predicted, nothing is worth attempting. He anticipates that conclusion and closes it off. Ignorance of the future is the very reason for decisive action, for generosity and for spread risks, not the reason to hold back.

He wanted the reader to recognise two kinds of knowledge. There are things we can know: that clouds full of water will rain and that a fallen tree stays where it fell, so some events are fixed once they have happened. And there are things we cannot know: the next disaster, the path of the wind, the way a child takes shape, which of two ventures will thrive. Wisdom is knowing which is which and acting accordingly. The farmer who watches the wind will never plant, because the wind will never tell him enough.

He also wanted a people who give. Whatever 'bread upon the waters' means in detail, it is about sending something valuable out of your own hands. A reader who takes in the whole book is meant to hold wealth loosely, spread it generously, and trust the God whose work no one can trace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These verses are mostly prescriptive, a string of commands, but they rest on description. The descriptions are the facts about clouds, trees and wind, and the confession of ignorance. The commands follow from them. We should keep the order: first we admit we cannot see the future, then we act with open hands.

The passage is not a promise of profit. 'You will find it again' is a proverb, a statement of how generosity often returns in God's time, not a contract. Reading it as a formula that giving always brings back more, and treating the passage as a method for getting rich, would run against the rest of the book, which sees wealth as a gift that cannot satisfy, Ecclesiastes 5:10. The warm side of the verse is that nothing given in faith is wasted, but the promise sits within God's freedom.

The passage is also not a licence for recklessness. Spreading a portion among seven or eight ventures is a counsel of prudence, and the same book that tells us to cast our bread also tells us to count the cost. What it rules out is the opposite error, hoarding and endless waiting. Applied today, it calls for generous giving, wise diversification and steady work, with prayer that God will give the increase, 1 Corinthians 3:6-7.

debates.question: Is 'cast your bread upon the waters' a call to charity or to commercial enterprise?

views.label: A call to generous giving
views.case: The Hebrew verb in verse 2 is the ordinary word 'give,' and the nearby proverbs praise the one who gives freely, Proverbs 11:24-25, and lends to the LORD in kindness to the poor, Proverbs 19:17. On this reading bread cast on the water is given to those who cannot repay, and its return is God's repayment. It is an old and common reading.

views.label: A call to bold trade
views.case: Bread on the waters pictures grain shipped by sea, and the advice to divide among seven or eight is the textbook advice for diversified risk. Verses 3 to 6 are about sowing and reaping, which are the language of enterprise. On this view the passage commends bold, spread out investment against an unknown future.

views.label: A single principle with two applications
views.case: Both readings lead to the same posture: let go of what you hold in order to gain what you cannot guarantee. The sower and the generous giver, the merchant and the lender, all part with what is in hand on the strength of what is not yet seen.

debates.bearing: The argument of the whole unit does not depend on the choice. Either way the Teacher is telling us to loosen the hand because the future is hidden. The reader who takes it as charity should not use it as an excuse for carelessness, and the reader who takes it as enterprise should not forget that the passage sits next to the book's insistence that wealth is a gift.

debates.question: What is the second thing we cannot know in verse 5, the wind or the spirit?

views.label: The path of the wind
views.case: The Hebrew word ruach can mean wind, breath or spirit. In the context of verse 4, which speaks of watching the wind, the natural reading is that the wind goes where no one can chart it. It is then set beside the mystery of how bones form in the womb.

views.label: The coming of the spirit into the bones
views.case: The BSB footnote gives an alternative: 'As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones.' Here the parallel is between the unseen spirit and the growing body, as in the way God puts breath into the bones of the valley in Ezekiel 37:5-6. This reading picks up the ruach of 12:7.

views.label: Deliberate double meaning
views.case: A word that can mean either wind or spirit, set between a weather verse and a womb verse, may be meant to be heard both ways. Jesus makes the same play when He says that 'the wind blows where it wishes,' and so it is with everyone born of the Spirit, John 3:8.

debates.bearing: Whichever the translation, the claim of verse 5 is that human understanding stops at the origins of life and movement, and that the one who makes all things is the one who knows. The word 'spirit' in the footnote anticipates what Ecclesiastes 12:7 says about the end of life, and the connection is part of the beauty.

debates.question: What is verse 3 doing between the commands?

views.label: A statement of what can be known
views.case: The clouds will rain and the tree will lie where it falls: these are fixed patterns that stand against the uncertainties that follow. A person who knows what can be known is free to act on it and to stop fretting about what cannot.

views.label: A picture of irreversible events
views.case: The fallen tree stays where it lies, as a sign that some things cannot be undone, so choices matter and deserve care. Some preachers have also read it as a figure for death fixing a person's state, though the passage does not say so.

debates.bearing: The verse is best taken as the settled ground from which the exhortation springs: nature has patterns we can trust and ends we cannot alter, and neither excuses idleness. It is a small lesson in telling the knowable from the unknowable.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verb in verse 1, translated 'cast,' is shalach, which is the ordinary Hebrew verb for send. It is the verb of Exodus 5:1, where Pharaoh is told to let the people go, and the same root appears in sending messengers and sending away. The bread is not thrown away but sent out, like a courier on an errand. And it is sent 'upon the face of the waters,' the literal sense of the phrase, so that it sails out of sight on the surface. The word 'find' that closes the line, matsa, is the same verb the book uses when it says that no one can find out or comprehend the work done under the sun, 8:17. What the mind cannot find, the hand finds.

In verse 2 the instruction to 'divide' is, in the Hebrew, the verb natan, 'give.' It is the ordinary word for gift, and it fits the charity reading as comfortably as the commercial. The phrase 'seven, or even eight' is a Hebrew numerical idiom, a number followed by its successor, found in Proverbs 6:16 and Micah 5:5. It means a full and generous count with a little over. The word for the 'disaster,' ra'ah, is the general word for evil or calamity, the same word used for the 'evil' the Teacher has described under the sun. The unknown is not neutral; it may be bad.

In verse 5 the word ruach carries the whole verse. It is wind, breath and spirit at once, and in the Hebrew the clause can be read as 'the way of the wind' or, as the BSB footnote reads, 'the way the spirit comes to the bones.' The same word closes the poem of 12:7, where the ruach returns to God who gave it. The verse also calls God 'the Maker of all things,' literally the one who makes 'the all,' ha-kol. This is the very word of 1:2 and 12:8, 'Everything is futile,' the all that is hevel. The Teacher holds the two statements side by side: the all is fleeting, and the all has a Maker.

Verse 6 closes with the verb of success, kasher, 'which will succeed,' the root behind the 'skill produces success' of 10:10. The command, 'do not rest your hands,' uses the root of rest, nuach. The hand is not to take its rest in the evening, because the evening sowing may be the one that prospers. And the last words, 'this or that,' zeh o zeh, and 'both alike,' ke-echad, show an openness to surprise: perhaps neither will thrive, perhaps both.

typology.type: The seed sown without knowing the harvest, 11:4, 11:6
typology.fulfillment: Jesus tells of the sower who scatters seed on every kind of ground, some lost and some bearing thirty, sixty or a hundredfold, Mark 4:3-8. And He tells of the seed that grows 'though he knows not how,' Mark 4:26-29, which is the Teacher's ignorance made into a parable of the kingdom. The type breaks at one point: the farmer in Ecclesiastes sows against bad luck, while the kingdom sower sows a word whose growth is secure because the soil is in God's hand. The harvest does not depend on the sower's vigilance.

typology.type: Bread sent out and found again after many days, 11:1
typology.fulfillment: The bread of the poor and the lender's kindness returns in God's time, Proverbs 19:17. In Christ the pattern deepens: He gives Himself where He cannot be repaid, and the Father repays 'at the resurrection of the righteous,' Luke 14:12-14. When Jesus gave bread to the crowd, the pieces left over filled twelve baskets, John 6:11-13, a small sign of bread that comes back more. The type falls short in that the Teacher's return is uncertain, while Christ's giving of Himself is answered by an empty tomb.

typology.type: The grain that falls into the ground, 11:6
typology.fulfillment: The farmer lets seed leave his hand with no assurance. Jesus says 'unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit,' John 12:24. Paul uses the same picture for resurrection: 'What you sow does not come to life unless it dies,' and God gives it a body as He has designed, 1 Corinthians 15:36-38. The type is not exact, for the farmer sows seed he can spare, whereas Christ sows Himself. But the shape is the same: loss in the ground, then life.

typology.type: The wind and the womb that no one can chart, 11:5
typology.fulfillment: Jesus tells Nicodemus that the wind blows where it wishes and 'so it is with everyone born of the Spirit,' John 3:8. The same unseen movement that formed a child in the womb forms new birth. Nicodemus could not trace it, and neither could the Teacher. The type falls short only in that Jesus tells us whose work it is, the Spirit's, so that what the Teacher called unknowable is named, though no less mysterious.

study.christ:
The Teacher's command to cast and to sow is a call to give up what we hold, trusting that we will find it again after many days. The whole shape of the gospel is that movement. 'Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, and He is the grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies in order to bear much fruit, John 12:24. The one who tells the parable of the sower is also the seed, and He is the first-fruits of a great harvest, 1 Corinthians 15:20. What the Teacher can only urge as a risk, Christ has done as a certainty, and the harvest has begun.

The passage leads to Him by the theme of giving to those who cannot repay. 'When you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind... you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous,' Luke 14:13-14. Repayment is placed beyond death, which is the only place that the promise of 'after many days' can be fully kept. The believer who gives to the poor is imitating the one who 'gave Himself up for us' as a fragrant offering, Ephesians 5:2, and is lending, in the proverb's words, to the LORD, who will repay.

The passage leads to Him by the matter of fear and boldness. In the parable of the talents the servant who buried his master's money out of fear is condemned, while the servants who put theirs to work are praised, Matthew 25:14-30. The servant who would not act on what he did not know is the picture of the man who watches the wind and never sows. Christ calls His people to be bold with what He gives, not because outcomes are guaranteed, but because He is trustworthy.

It leads to Him by the Spirit. The unseen path of the wind and the spirit coming to the bones is, in the New Testament, the Spirit's work in new birth, John 3:8, and in Ezekiel's vision the breath enters the bones and they live, Ezekiel 37:5-6. The work of God that no one can trace has been made known in part: God has put His Spirit in those who belong to Him.

Finally He is the answer to the anxiety underneath the passage. 'Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself,' Matthew 6:34. The Teacher's refrain of not knowing could lead to dread, but Jesus points to the Father who feeds the birds that do not sow or reap, Matthew 6:26. A word of care: the passage does not name Christ, and the bread on the waters is not a hidden picture of the Last Supper. The links are the New Testament's own use of sowing, giving and the Spirit, and they show where the Teacher's counsel finds its footing.
study.god:
The passage names God only once, in verse 5, but its weight rests on that verse. He is 'the Maker of all things,' and His work is the thing that cannot be understood. The Teacher does not say that God is hidden because He is absent. He says that His works run deeper than any observer can follow. 'The secret things belong to the LORD our God,' Deuteronomy 29:29. That is a statement of God's greatness, as Isaiah says, 'His understanding is beyond searching out,' Isaiah 40:28.

God is the one who governs the weather and the wind. He 'causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth' and 'brings forth the wind from His storehouses,' Psalm 135:7. He gives 'rain from heaven and fruitful seasons,' Acts 14:17, and has promised that 'seedtime and harvest... shall never cease,' Genesis 8:22. The Teacher's farmer who cannot read the wind lives under a Lord who sends it. The clouds that seem random are in His hands.

He is the God who forms life in secret. The psalmist who says 'You knit me together in my mother's womb' and Job who says 'Your hands shaped me' speak of the same mystery that the Teacher confesses, Psalm 139:13 and Job 10:8. Where the Teacher says we cannot understand, they respond with praise. Both are right. What we cannot trace we can worship.

He is the one who gives the increase. 'I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow,' 1 Corinthians 3:6. This is why work is not futile even when its results are hidden. The farmer's job is to sow and the Lord's to give the harvest, and a man's heart may plan his course but 'the LORD determines his steps,' Proverbs 16:9.

He is generous. 'Every good and perfect gift is from above,' James 1:17, and the one who gives bread to others is imitating the one who gives bread to all. He supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, 2 Corinthians 9:10. A person who spreads out their portion among many is reflecting the character of a God who scatters rain on the just and the unjust.

The tension in the passage is that God is wholly sovereign while the future is wholly unknown to us, and we are still told to work. These are not in conflict. Sovereignty is the reason we can sow without anxiety, and our ignorance is the reason we must sow in trust. For worship, the passage calls for confident, unhurried obedience. We do not need to see the harvest to be faithful. We need only to know the Maker, and to put our hands to the seed.

crossReferences.note: 'One gives freely, yet gains even more.' The proverb is the plainest parallel to Ecclesiastes 11:1-2. It sets scattering against hoarding and promises that the generous will be refreshed. Like the Teacher's verse, it is a statement of how God's world tends to work and not a contractual guarantee.

'Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.' This gives the charity reading of bread cast on the waters a theological base. The one who gives to the poor is lending to God, and the return is not at the mercy of the waves.

'Blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters.' The sowing beside water here sounds like Ecclesiastes 11:1, and the word 'blessed' marks it as a good place to be. It adds weight to the reading that bread on the waters is seed, sown with hope and expected to grow.

'Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy.' The sower goes out with seed, in tears, and comes back with sheaves. It treats the sowing as costly and the harvest as a gift, which is the shape of the Teacher's command to sow without knowing which will succeed.

Paul tells us that God is not mocked and whatever a man sows he reaps, and 'let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest.' It adds a clause the Teacher leaves out, the 'if we do not give up,' and gives the harvest to the right season.

Whoever sows generously will reap generously, and God 'supplies seed to the sower and bread for food.' Paul sets the Teacher's counsel in the context of a love offering and names the source of both seed and bread. The giver is himself a recipient.

Jesus tells His host to invite those who cannot repay, for 'you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.' It names the time of the harvest that Ecclesiastes 11:1 calls 'many days.' Repayment lies in the resurrection, and the one who gives is not left without return.

The seed sprouts and grows 'though he knows not how.' The farmer sleeps and wakes, and the earth produces the crop. The man of Ecclesiastes 11:5 who does not know how bones form is matched by the man who does not know how seed grows, and both are told to get on with the work.

'The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going.' Jesus uses the Teacher's own image, the unchartable wind, and gives it a name: the Spirit who gives new birth. The word ruach in Ecclesiastes 11:5 becomes pneuma in the Gospel.

The Lord says to the bones, 'I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life.' It is the nearest Old Testament account of breath coming to bones, and it supports the footnote reading of Ecclesiastes 11:5. What no man can explain, God does.

'You do not even know what will happen tomorrow!' James addresses merchants who plan a year of trade without thinking of God and tells them to say, 'If the Lord is willing.' He applies the Teacher's ignorance as humility and not as a reason to stop planning.

The servant who hid his talent in the ground for fear was called wicked and lazy, and the others who put theirs to work were praised. It is the Teacher's warning about the man who watches the wind and never sows, spoken by the Lord, who judges how His servants handled what He gave.

study.oneStory:
From the opening pages of Scripture, the human calling was to work and keep a garden, to sow and to tend, in a world whose rain and growth were God's gift. Genesis 8:22 promises that seedtime and harvest will never cease, and the story of Israel is a story of farmers and shepherds, of tithes and first fruits, and of a people taught to give. The Torah sets the pattern of the open hand: the gleaning left for the poor, the loan to the needy, the offering from the field. Ecclesiastes 11:1-6 stands in that line.

It also stands at a particular moment in the book's story. After ten chapters that look hard at what no one can know, the Teacher refuses the path of despair. He gives a path of faith: sow, give, spread the risk, and leave the rest to God. In the Bible's larger story this is the posture of Abraham, who went out 'without knowing where he was going,' Hebrews 11:8, and who gave up the thing he held most dear. It is the posture of the faithful in Hebrews 11 who did not receive what was promised but trusted in the one who promised.

The whole story hinges on a seed. The promise of a seed in Genesis 3:15 and Genesis 22:18 is the promise that God will bring a harvest out of a barren world. In Christ the seed falls into the ground. He gives Himself away with no certainty from any human point of view, and He is found again after three days, John 12:24. Because He rose, Paul can close the great chapter on resurrection with this charge: 'Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain,' 1 Corinthians 15:58. What the Teacher told us to do by faith, the apostle tells us to do by knowledge.

The end of the story is a harvest. The one who sows in tears comes home with sheaves, Psalm 126:6. The bread cast on the waters of a thousand acts of kindness is found again, and 'in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up,' Galatians 6:9. In the new creation there is no more disaster to fear, no more uncertain wind, and no more evil upon the land. The Maker of all things, whose work could not be traced, makes all things new, Revelation 21:5. The sowing hand is answered by a hand that wipes every tear away.

quiz.q: Why does the Teacher tell us to divide our portion among seven or even eight?

options.text: Because we do not know what disaster may befall the land, so we spread the risk in faith.
options.note: The unknown future is the stated reason for diversified, generous action.

options.text: Because it is wise not to stake everything on a single venture.
options.note: True to the picture, though the deeper point is trusting God with an unknown future.

options.text: Because seven and eight are sacred numbers to be obeyed exactly.
options.note: The numbers picture spreading widely, not a fixed rule to follow literally.

options.text: Because wealth should be hidden and hoarded against hard times.
options.note: The Teacher commends open-handed venture, not hoarding.

quiz.q: What is the danger in watching the wind and observing the clouds?

options.text: Endless caution never acts, so he will fail to sow and fail to reap.
options.note: Waiting for perfect conditions leads to paralysis and no harvest.

options.text: Studying the weather too long delays the necessary work.
options.note: A fair reading, though the sharper point is that overcaution never acts at all.

options.text: Farmers should ignore the weather completely.
options.note: The point is not to despise wisdom but not to be paralyzed by uncertainty.

options.text: The wind and clouds are evil omens to be feared.
options.note: They are simply pictures of uncertainty, not omens.

quiz.q: How does not knowing the work of God shape our action here?

options.text: Because His work is beyond us, we act in faith and leave the outcome to Him rather than freezing.
options.note: Confessed ignorance becomes the ground of trusting, diligent action.

options.text: Since we cannot understand God's work, we should trust Him with the results.
options.note: True, though it leaves out the active call to sow diligently anyway.

options.text: Since we cannot understand God's work, there is no point in trying anything.
options.note: This is the paralysis the passage explicitly rejects.

options.text: We can master the future if we study hard enough.
options.note: The passage says the opposite; the work of God cannot be traced out.

quiz.q: What does it mean to sow your seed in the morning and not rest your hands in the evening?

options.text: Work diligently and widely, for you do not know which effort will succeed.
options.note: Persistent, generous labor is commended because outcomes are hidden.

options.text: Keep working through the whole day without stopping to rest.
options.note: It commends diligence, but the point is breadth of effort under uncertainty, not literal sleeplessness.

options.text: Only the morning sowing really matters.
options.note: The Teacher says to sow at both times because either or both may prosper.

options.text: Effort is pointless because everything is uncertain.
options.note: The passage calls for more effort, not less, in the face of uncertainty.

quiz.q: How do these verses point forward to Christ?

options.text: He is the sower and the seed who fell into the ground and died to bear much fruit, so our labor in Him is never wasted.
options.note: Christ fulfills the picture of seed sown toward an unseen but certain harvest.

options.text: Jesus taught about sowing seed and giving generously.
options.note: True, and He is Himself the grain of wheat that died and rose, which the answer should reach.

options.text: The passage has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The seed and harvest imagery runs straight to Jesus in the Gospels.

options.text: It teaches that Christ guarantees every venture will make us rich.
options.note: It promises a harvest in God's hands, not guaranteed earthly profit.

questions: Where is fear of the unknown keeping you from acting, and what would it look like to cast your bread on the waters and trust God with the return?
The Teacher says to spread your portion widely and give generously. Where might God be calling you to open your hands rather than clutch what you have?
You cannot trace the work of God any more than you can chart the wind. How does admitting what you cannot know actually free you to act in faith today?
Which effort in your life are you tempted to abandon because you cannot see the outcome, and how could you keep sowing morning and evening?
Jesus is the seed that fell and died to bear much fruit. How does trusting that no labor in Him is wasted change the way you work and give this week?

translationNotes.note: Cast your bread upon the waters has been read both as seaborne trade that returns a profit and as generous giving that God repays after many days; the Hebrew lechem means bread, food, or grain.
Divide your portion among seven, or even eight uses cheleq, the book's word for one's God-given share; seven or eight is a way of saying spread it widely, do not risk it all in one place.

A footnote in some editions renders the line as you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones; the same Hebrew word means both wind and spirit or breath, deepening the mystery of the work of God.
